title: Practice what you preach
hookLine: let deeds match words, and be the same person everywhere (Letters 20)

lines: THE INTERVIEW. THE TRAFFIC. THE MIDNIGHT POST.
A DIFFERENT CHARACTER FOR EACH ROOM.
cards: Picture the person you are in a job interview. Now the person you are in traffic. Now the one who answers the phone when it's your mother, and the one who types a comment under a stranger's post at midnight.
Same name on all four. Are they the same person? Plenty of people run a small repertory company, a different character for each room.
Seneca noticed it in himself and in his friend Lucilius, and in the twentieth letter he names the test he thinks matters most. It isn't what you know. It's whether the rooms agree.

teach.b: In Latin the sentence is five words and a comma: facere docet philosophia, non dicere. Philosophy teaches us to do, not to say. Seneca isn't against words; he spent a lifetime writing them.
He's against words that never leave the page.

teach.h: ARE THE SPEECH AND THE LIFE IN TUNE?
teach.b: So he tells Lucilius to ask whether his speech and his life are in tune, whether his conduct at home matches what he says in public, whether he is the same person in every room.
A person can make a lovely speech about patience and then snap at a waiter. The speech was true. The speaker wasn't, yet.
Then Seneca's short definition of wisdom: always to want the same things, and always to refuse the same things. Not a new goal every week, not one set of values for friends and another for strangers.
The things you choose stay chosen. And an honest twist.
Seneca was one of the richest men in Rome, and critics in his own day said so loudly. He knew his life lagged behind his letters.
Elsewhere he admits he writes as a patient in the same hospital, not as the doctor. So the rule isn't a boast. It's a direction, set by someone who also hadn't arrived.
The gap between your words and your deeds isn't proof you're a fraud. It's the distance left to walk.

how: Readers of Seneca often take one principle they have stated aloud and check, at the end of the day, whether one action matched it.

o: never changing your mind about anything
acting at home the way you speak in public
keeping one routine every single day

games.q: the twentieth letter — tap the pairs.

s: Seneca says words don't matter at all
he wrote hundreds of pages; his point is that words must turn into deeds.
Seneca defines wisdom as always wanting and refusing the same things
the same values in every room, not a new set each week.
Seneca claimed he had fully lived up to his own teaching
he admits his life lags behind; he writes as a fellow patient.

games.q: you just told a friend you're working on patience. ten minutes later a waiter brings the wrong order. what does Seneca's test ask?
o: whether your speech was well put.
whether your deed matched your word.
whether the waiter heard your speech.
games.why: philosophy teaches doing, not saying: the test is whether the rooms agree.

practice: Choose one thing you've said lately and meant, like I want to be more patient, or I'll call more often. Picture one specific room and person later today where that word could become a deed, in its small version, not the heroic one.

wordCard.voice: Same person: Seneca's test of whether your conduct at home matches what you say in public, in every room you enter. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the same everywhere. One self in the interview, in traffic and at midnight. Until tomorrow.
